n: Paul anticipates an objection: if being a “real Jew” is inward, is there any advantage to being Jewish or circumcised at all?
Yes, much! Above all, the Jews were entrusted with God’s revelations — the scriptures. That was a priceless stewardship.

f.g: God’s spoken words — the revealed scriptures.

f.w: unto them were committed the oracles of God

n: What if some were unfaithful? Does their unfaithfulness cancel God’s faithfulness? Paul asks whether human failure can break God’s promises.

f.g: God’s faithfulness, his reliability in keeping promises.

n: Absolutely not! God stays true even if every person proves false. Paul quotes David’s psalm of repentance: God is right when he speaks and wins when he is judged.

f.g: Greek mē genoito — “May it never be!” — Paul’s strongest denial.

f.w: That thou mightest be justified in thy sayings

n: Another objection: if our wrongdoing makes God’s righteousness shine brighter, isn’t God unfair to punish us? Paul admits he is voicing a human argument.

f.g: I’m using a human way of reasoning.

n: Of course not — otherwise how could God judge the world at all?

f.w: how shall God judge the world?

n: The objector presses: if my lie ends up glorifying God by contrast, why am I still judged as a sinner?
Some critics even claimed Paul taught, “Let’s do evil so good may come.” Paul calls this a slander, and says those who reason that way deserve condemnation.
So are we Jews better off morally? Not at all. Paul has already shown that Jews and Gentiles alike are all under the power of sin.
Paul strings together Old Testament verses, starting with: “There is none righteous, no, not one.” No one can claim to be sinless on their own.

f.w: There is none righteous, no, not one

n: No one truly understands or seeks God on their own.

f.w: there is none that seeketh after God

n: All have turned aside and become worthless together; no one does good, not even one.

f.g: Useless, gone bad — like spoiled milk.

n: The quotations now describe sinful speech: throats like open graves, tongues that deceive, lips with snake venom.

f.w: Their throat is an open sepulchre
the poison of asps is under their lips

n: Their mouths are full of cursing and bitterness.

f.w: Whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness

n: Then sinful actions: their feet rush to shed blood.

f.w: Their feet are swift to shed blood

n: Ruin and misery follow wherever they go.

f.w: Destruction and misery are in their ways

n: They have never known the path of peace.

f.w: the way of peace have they not known

n: The root of it all: they have no reverence for God. Without respect for God, everything else unravels.

f.w: There is no fear of God before their eyes

n: These scriptures speak to those under the law — the Jews — so that every mouth is silenced and the whole world stands accountable before God.

f.g: Every excuse silenced, as in a courtroom.

n: No one is made right with God by keeping the law, because the law’s role is to make us aware of sin. A mirror shows the dirt but can’t wash it away.

f.w: by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified
by the law is the knowledge of sin

n: “But now” — the great turning point. God’s way of making people righteous has been revealed apart from the law, though the law and prophets testified of it.

f.g: A pivotal shift from humanity’s problem to God’s solution.

f.w: witnessed by the law and the prophets

n: This righteousness comes through faith in Jesus Christ, for all who believe — with no distinction between Jew and Gentile.

f.g: Can mean faith in Christ or the faithfulness of Christ — both are true.

n: Everyone has sinned and falls short of God’s glory. This is one of the Bible’s best-known verses on the universal need for a Savior.
But we are made right with God freely, as a gift of grace, through the redemption Christ provides. “Redemption” means buying someone out of slavery.

f.g: Release by payment of a ransom.

n: God set Christ forth as the atoning sacrifice, received through faith in his blood. This showed God’s justice, since he had patiently passed over earlier sins.

f.g: Greek hilastērion — the place or means of atonement; the word for the “mercy seat” on the ark.

n: God shows he is both just and the one who justifies believers in Jesus. Through Christ, justice is satisfied and mercy is extended — both at once.

f.w: that he might be just, and the justifier

n: So where is there room for boasting? None at all. Not by a law of works, but by the “law of faith.” We can’t take credit for a gift.

Paul concludes that a person is made right with God by faith, not by the works of the law of Moses. The Joseph Smith Translation reads “by faith alone without the deeds of the law,” keeping the focus on the Mosaic law.

f.w: justified by faith without the deeds of the law

f.g: The works of the law of Moses — rituals like circumcision, not good works in general.

n: Is God only the God of the Jews? Isn’t he also the God of Gentiles? Yes, of course!

f.w: is he not also of the Gentiles?

n: Since there is only one God, he justifies Jews and Gentiles in the same way — through faith.
Does faith cancel the law? Not at all! Faith establishes the law — it fulfills the law’s true purpose of pointing to Christ.
